items.titleTr: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
items.summaryTr: The reported strikes come a day after Ukraine launched its largest recorded drone attack on Russia since the start of the war, according to Moscow.
items.articleText: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says - Published Two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital have reportedly been struck in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The missiles hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges spanning the Dnipro River, Klitschko said, adding that water and power supplies had been disrupted. Meanwhile, Ukraine struck the landmark Kerch Bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea killing two people, the region's Moscow-installed governor said. President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier warned that Moscow might launch further strikes on the country on Monday night, after Ukrainian, US and European officials held further talks aimed at ending the years-long conflict. Those online talks, attended by US envoy Jared Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, came after Russia said it recorded the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began. Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems". "Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added. Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services have been damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters. Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids. Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv. An estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city. Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October. Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials. Separately, the Ukrainian military struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second consecutive day, the region's Moscow-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said on Telegram. Traffic across the bridge had been suspended, he added. The landmark bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. Russian President Vladimir Putin inaugurated the bridge to great fanfare in 2018. The severity of the latest strike on Kerch Bridge is still unclear, though it is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences. Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said. The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war. Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership. He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future". In an address on Monday evening, Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes. Zelensky said that Europe was represented for the first time by the full delegation that will participate in negotiations with Moscow - including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the EU and Nato. The Ukrainian president has long called for European delegates to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union. He also said that Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea. Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72. Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022. Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit. Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel". Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control. items.titleTr: Vance says he will decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 US presidential run
items.summaryTr: The US vice-president tells Fox News that when he makes a decision to run or otherwise, he will "be all in on whatever that decision is".
items.articleText: Vance says he will decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 US presidential run - Published US Vice-President JD Vance has said he will make a decision "sometime next year" about whether or not he will run for president in 2028. In an interview with Fox News, Vance would not provide a timeline on making a determination, but signaled he is not in a hurry to make up his mind. "I haven't made a decision. We'll figure it out sometime next year," Vance said. When pressed by host Laura Ingraham, he added: "When I make a decision, I'll be all in on whatever that decision is." The comments came amid growing interest in Vance's next moves in the weeks since voters handed both President Donald Trump and Republicans a resounding defeat in the midterm elections. People in Vance's orbit who have spoken to the BBC said the November elections did not change the timeline around his decision-making process for 2028. He is expected to run but allies believe he could wait several months to make a final decision. Speculation about Vance's White House aspirations began the moment President Trump selected him as his 2024 running mate. The pick positioned Vance, who entered the White House as one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, as the most likely heir to Trump's Make America Great Again (Maga) movement. But while serving in office, Vance has carefully avoided discussing his own political ambitions. He kept that up during the midterms, when supporters frequently interrupted his campaign speeches to urge him to run in 2028. Vance's stock response was that Republicans needed to focus on the election at hand in November. But with the midterms in the rearview mirror, and Republicans eager to move on from their 2026 drubbing, the next election at hand is now the 2028 presidential race. - Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war - Published5 November - The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now? - Published8 November Vance would likely jump to the top of the Republican primary field whenever he launches his bid, should he choose to run. But the contest is expected to be a competitive process with a large field of candidates. Numerous other high-profile Republicans are rumoured to be interested in running or have said publicly that they are mulling a White House bid. The list includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, outgoing Florida Governor and 2024 hopeful Ron DeSantis, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, among others. Trump has praised Vance and Rubio on several occasions, while also insisting that he is not sure who he will endorse in 2028 - or if he will weigh in at all. The president's endorsement would be influential with the Maga base. But the midterms revealed widespread frustration with many of his second-term policies, complicating the path forward for potential candidates like Vance who are tied to Trump's agenda. Vance blamed the midterm results on the war with Iran in a post-election social media post. In it, he also mapped out a plan for winning back Republican voters, which included ending the war and focusing on the economy. The message was widely seen as a first step by Vance to distance himself from Trump ahead of a 2028 run. In the Fox News interview, Vance reiterated his view that the war came with a "political cost", but said it has not damaged his relationship with Trump. "There's no daylight" on the Iran war between Trump and senior administration officials including himself, Vance said. He added that Trump would not let the conflict become a "forever war" and said the administration would not let the war, which was launched by the US and Israel in February 2026, even become "a two-year commitment". Vance also discussed the nationwide air traffic outrage last week, which brought air travel across the US to a standstill for several hours. The vice-president called on lawmakers to fix the issue in the final weeks of the current congressional session. He also touched on the scandal engulfing Nvidia, its former CEO Jensen Huang and its implications for US-China relations. Vance said there was still no "clarity" about the accuracy of reports that a woman with whom Huang reportedly had an affair with was indeed a Chinese spy. "There is a lack of clarity about it. I don't know and [Trump] doesn't know whether this woman was a spy or not," Vance said. Related topics - Published6 November - Published7 November - Published4 November

In an interview with Fox News, Vance would not provide a timeline on making a determination, but signaled he is not in a hurry to make up his mind. "I haven't made a decision. We'll figure it out sometime next year," Vance said. When pressed by host Laura Ingraham, he added: "When I make a decision, I'll be all in on whatever that decision is." The comments came amid growing interest in Vance's next moves in the weeks since voters handed both President Donald Trump and Republicans a resounding defeat in the midterm elections. People in Vance's orbit who have spoken to the BBC said the November elections did not change the timeline around his decision-making process for 2028. He is expected to run but allies believe he could wait several months to make a final decision. Speculation about Vance's White House aspirations began the moment President Trump selected him as his 2024 running mate. The pick positioned Vance, who entered the White House as one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, as the most likely heir to Trump's Make America Great Again (Maga) movement. But while serving in office, Vance has carefully avoided discussing his own political ambitions. He kept that up during the midterms, when supporters frequently interrupted his campaign speeches to urge him to run in 2028. Vance's stock response was that Republicans needed to focus on the election at hand in November. But with the midterms in the rearview mirror, and Republicans eager to move on from their 2026 drubbing, the next election at hand is now the 2028 presidential race. - Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war - Published5 November - The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now? - Published8 November Vance would likely jump to the top of the Republican primary field whenever he launches his bid, should he choose to run. But the contest is expected to be a competitive process with a large field of candidates. Numerous other high-profile Republicans are rumoured to be interested in running or have said publicly that they are mulling a White House bid. The list includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, outgoing Florida Governor and 2024 hopeful Ron DeSantis, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, among others. Trump has praised Vance and Rubio on several occasions, while also insisting that he is not sure who he will endorse in 2028 - or if he will weigh in at all. The president's endorsement would be influential with the Maga base. But the midterms revealed widespread frustration with many of his second-term policies, complicating the path forward for potential candidates like Vance who are tied to Trump's agenda. Vance blamed the midterm results on the war with Iran in a post-election social media post. In it, he also mapped out a plan for winning back Republican voters, which included ending the war and focusing on the economy. The message was widely seen as a first step by Vance to distance himself from Trump ahead of a 2028 run. In the Fox News interview, Vance reiterated his view that the war came with a "political cost", but said it has not damaged his relationship with Trump. "There's no daylight" on the Iran war between Trump and senior administration officials including himself, Vance said. He added that Trump would not let the conflict become a "forever war" and said the administration would not let the war, which was launched by the US and Israel in February 2026, even become "a two-year commitment". Vance also discussed the nationwide air traffic outrage last week, which brought air travel across the US to a standstill for several hours. The vice-president called on lawmakers to fix the issue in the final weeks of the current congressional session. He also touched on the scandal engulfing Nvidia, its former CEO Jensen Huang and its implications for US-China relations. Vance said there was still no "clarity" about the accuracy of reports that a woman with whom Huang reportedly had an affair with was indeed a Chinese spy. "There is a lack of clarity about it. I don't know and [Trump] doesn't know whether this woman was a spy or not," Vance said. Related topics - Published6 November - Published7 November - Published4 November

items.titleTr: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex CEO
items.summaryTr: A number of tech figures have backed an effort asking the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
items.articleText: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex CEO - Published Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort. Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign. But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy. The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted. Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return. The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive. They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process". Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back. Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report. The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. New rules The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models. The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development. The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China. The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said. Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US. He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company". In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington. - How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? - Published4 days ago - How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House - Published3 days ago The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad. The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore. Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent. But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors. Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns. But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere. While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry. US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost. Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair. Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said. The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump. 'A handshake with Jensen' Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question." But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine". Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm. Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading. In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang". Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation. For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday. - Published1 day ago

items.titleTr: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
items.summaryTr: Pakistan's ex-prime minister, who has been in prison since August 2023, says he has been denied justice.
items.articleText: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive' - Published Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating. "At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar. Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health. Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated. Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action. In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage". He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery. "I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote. He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health. He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year. "I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote. Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing". "[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters. Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable". Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things. At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence. Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics. Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

items.titleTr: Customers report service outages at major US banks
items.summaryTr: Chase Bank, the largest US bank, said a software bug might be causing the issue, but that it was not "systemic'" or "cyber-related".
items.articleText: Customers report service outages at major US banks - Published Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services. Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related". Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening. The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage, a network failure that grounded all US flights, and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage". Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website. Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News. A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details. - Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage - Published3 days ago - Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech - Published3 days ago Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds". The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US. The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank. Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported. Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions. US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent. Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments. Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted. As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages. Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights". That issue resolved within a few hours. The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity. The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines. The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), but comes as other industries report different outages around the US. On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues. The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel. Additional reporting by Max Matza. Related topics - Published1 day ago
